MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
Here's everything, starting with tomorrow's route, since it has no slack at the end.

## Tomorrow's route: B, then A, then C

This is the only order that works. B must be finished by 09:30, so it has to come first, and C can't start before 11:00, so it has to come last.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B** (20 min drive) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B ✅ done 25 min before the 09:30 opening |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive B to A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at **A** ✅ inside the 09:00–10:00 window |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive A to C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break** near C, while waiting for it to open |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at **C** ✅ |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive C to depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot, with zero minutes to spare** |

**The problem is the return.** C can't start before 11:00, and unloading plus the drive home takes exactly an hour, so the van gets back at 12:00 on the dot in every possible order. Any delay at C, or any traffic on the way back, makes him late.

I've also assumed the drive from C back to the depot takes 45 minutes, the same as the drive out. If it takes longer, the plan doesn't work at all.

Options to build in some margin:

- **Ask C whether they'd accept 10:45** (he's nearby from 10:25 anyway).
- **Check whether "back by 12:00" can flex** by 15 minutes.
- **Have the driver phone C a few minutes before 11:00** so they're ready at the door and unloading starts promptly.

The rest of the route has slack: 25 minutes at B and 15 minutes at A. The break fits naturally into the wait before C.

## Van names

- **Chip 'n' Dale** (as in Chippendale)
- **Dovetail**
- **Vanity Fair**
- **The Sideboard Express**
- **Hepplewhite Van**

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], your delivery from [Business] is on its way and should be with you in about [20] minutes. Please make sure someone's in to receive it. Thanks!

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Condition.** Check for scratches, dents or marks in the finish from the journey. A quick comparison with pre-delivery photos settles any later dispute.
2. **Completeness.** Make sure every part is there: shelves, keys, handles, castors, glass panels and fixings.
3. **Function and stability.** Open and close drawers and doors, and check the piece stands level and steady where the customer wants it.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed by default.** It's easier to store and search, it can include photos of the piece as delivered, and it can't be lost. Keep paper as a backup for customers without email, or for anyone who asks for it. Either way, capture the customer's signature at the door, on a phone or tablet or on the paper copy.

## Proof of delivery, in one line

> **Proof of delivery** is a record, usually a signature, photo or both, showing an item was handed over to the right person, at the right address, at a given time and in good condition.

## Evening-before text (under 160 characters)

> Hi Sam, Oakleaf Restoration here! Your furniture arrives tomorrow between 9:30 and 10:30. We'll text when we're on our way. Reply to rearrange. Thanks!

That example is **151 characters**. With your own details, keep the customer's name and your business name to **31 characters combined** or fewer, and it will stay under 160.

**Use plain straight apostrophes**, as in "We'll" typed directly on a keyboard. Curly apostrophes, special symbols and emojis switch most phones to a different text encoding with a 70-character limit, which splits the message into two or three texts.

For tomorrow's customers, rough windows would be: **B** around 08:45–09:15, **A** around 09:15–09:45, and **C** at 11:00.
